h: The religion of smoke: in Delhi, breathing is a political decision
dek: In The Wire, Tikender Singh Panwar writes that a politics that turned fireworks into faith, and any question about pollution into anti-Hinduism, has robbed Delhi of its air, and the price is paid by those who cannot leave.
body: Tikender Singh Panwar, who reached Delhi two days after Diwali, writes that even 48 hours later the air had not cleared. According to the meteorological institute, fireworks made up more than 80 per cent of the pollution. Meanwhile the Union minister and the chief minister were seen on a flower-decked Yamuna cruise. In a city gasping for breath, the government inaugurated a boat.

In Nagpur, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said old fireworks carried no poison, that they kept insects away and that ghee lamps purified the air, and that there was science in all this. On the night of 8 November it was not seventeenth-century fireworks that burned but factory-made ones full of chemicals and metals. Summoning the old to justify the present is not science, it is memory wearing a cloak.

This is not a slip, it is a pattern. For three or four days after Diwali the fireworks kept going past midnight, and in which neighbourhoods is not hard to work out. In 2023 a Delhi BJP leader took pride in fireworks, and the state president called the Supreme Court's permission for green crackers a victory for sanatan dharma.

Maneka Gandhi had said there is no such thing as a green cracker, while Delhi burns fireworks worth Rs 800 crore. Accountability runs backwards: more than 200 police cases were filed for breaking the rules, but no big name was touched. The law falls on those who do not know it; those who clapped from the stage walk away.

Doctors say something else. Randeep Guleria tells people to leave Delhi in the worst weeks; a former AIIMS pulmonologist asked asthma and heart patients to stay away for six to eight weeks, if they can. That 'if' is the whole point. A professor goes to his daughter in Pune; labourers and street vendors stay here and drink the same air.

The writer's route starts from below. The ward committees promised by the 74th constitutional amendment have still not arrived. Had they worked, this debate would not be a fight between two parties on television but an argument between neighbours and a school principal. The strongest weapon is data that belongs to the people: measuring devices in every ward.
nazar: Everyone has a right to Delhi's air, but responsibility is pinned only on those with no way out. The leaders who call fireworks faith from a stage and then inaugurate a cruise are the ones deciding whom the law will touch.

In Deshkaal's view, the only thing that can stand up to a politics that calls clean air anti-Hindu is open data and neighbourhood accountability. Before a case against someone who lit a cracker, there should be a question for those who handed him a certificate of faith.
sawal: Who will bring the clappers to the dock?
ref: 74th amendment
A 1992 amendment that gave constitutional status to urban bodies and provided for ward committees. Most states never implemented it.
Green crackers
Low-pollution fireworks allowed after a Supreme Court order. Maneka Gandhi and many others say they are not pollution-free either.
ank: Police cases for breaking firework rules

h: Smog does not see borders; the two need one table
dek: Dawn's editorial says there is no winning the race to be the most polluted between Delhi and Lahore; shared data and shared investigation are the only way.
body: On Friday Delhi became the world's most polluted major city and Lahore slipped to seventh. Dawn's editorial says this ranking is no comfort to those breathing the air. A change in the wind can improve a city's number, but the sources of pollution stay where they are.

The smog over northern India and Pakistan comes from vehicle exhaust, factories, dust and crop residue burnt in the fields. In winter a warm layer of air traps the dirt below. That is, most of it is homegrown, and both governments have work to do at home.

Satellites saw 18,825 fire spots in Pakistan's Punjab, most of them tied to burning crop residue. In a recent 40-day stretch, Lahore stayed above the national standard for fine particles every single day. Officials speak of more raids, fines and shutting polluting units. The editorial agrees action is needed, but says its effect must last beyond the smog season.

Then there is a regional angle no government can dodge. Dirty air does not ask for a border, whatever the relations. Pakistan's climate minister is coming to Delhi for an SCO civilisational dialogue. The meeting was not called for pollution, but it is a chance for a serious conversation with Indian officials.

At the very least the two countries can share air-quality data, forecasts, health advisories and satellite images of farm fires. Scientists can look together at how pollution crosses the border. This cooperation does not wait for a grand treaty, and no one should be allowed the excuse that all the dirt is the neighbour's. The SCO platform already exists; the minister should use it.
nazar: For India this conversation is both easy and necessary. Cooperation on smog has little political win or loss, and the cost of sharing data is close to nothing. Governments that cannot save their cities from being the most polluted can at least stop hiding from each other.
If scientists from both countries sit at one table, it will also become clear how much of each city's air belongs to whom. That moves the argument to data, and away from accusations.
sawal: Why do the two countries not hold the smog numbers together?
ref: SCO
Shanghai Cooperation Organisation: a security and economic forum of China, Russia, India, Pakistan and Central Asian states.
Fine particles
PM2.5, particles smaller than 2.5 microns, which reach the lungs and the blood.

h: The encounter is quick, the trial is slow. Why?
dek: Meeran Chadha Borwankar, a former director general of the Bureau of Police Research, writes that bulldozers, SITs and special courts are jugaad, not a cure for the burden of four crore cases.
body: Indian courts have more than four crore criminal cases pending. The same government has been in power at the Centre for twelve years, yet there is no thought-through plan to shrink that mountain. In 2024 government data, 89.8 per cent of rape cases and 92.7 per cent of murder cases were still in court.

The writer says this jugaad is not only the poor citizen's compulsion, it is also the habit of governments. One state gives the police a free hand against crimes on women, another runs on half encounters with bullets in the leg, another sends the bulldozer. Settling crime outside the law means losing faith in your own justice system.

The real repair involves five agencies: police, forensics, prosecution, courts and prisons. All are badly short of staff, and the ordinary person pays for that every day. Recruitment must come with continuous training and new equipment. Forensic labs struggle with old technology, and cyber crime has grown so fast that many complaints are buried before they are even registered.

Special investigation teams are the same jugaad in another shape. Maharashtra has so many SITs running that even ministers do not have a count. A team is formed for every big incident and good investigators are pulled off ordinary people's cases. Special courts take the same judges and staff; resources are not added, only divided.

The writer offers a way. In July to September 2026, unemployment among people above 15 was 5.1 per cent. Hiring in the justice system will create jobs at every level. Fixing the whole machinery would take roughly five years. She asks why a state that can show such force against insurgency cannot give five years to its courts.
nazar: Bulldozers and encounters look cheap because their cost never shows up on the court's calendar. But every jugaad breaks a link in the law and weakens faith in it.
Hiring in the justice system is the least discussed and the most effective reform. It will cost money, but encounters and bulldozers are not free either.
sawal: If the courts can be fixed in five years, why the wait?
ref: SIT
Special Investigation Team, a dedicated team formed in every big case, which pulls investigators away from ordinary cases.
PLFS
The Periodic Labour Force Survey, the government survey that gives quarterly employment and unemployment figures.

h: Drones over the paddy field: who will be the farmer?
dek: Rukhsat Afrin writes that young people in Bangladesh are fleeing farming while graduates sit unemployed in cities, and both problems have one cure.
body: In Bangladesh the month of Agrahayan begins with golden paddy fields, the smell of new rice and the Nabanna festival. Behind that joy is a hard reality. White-collar jobs are not growing as fast as young people are coming out with degrees, and AI and automation are cutting roles in companies.

On the other side, farming, which has fed millions for decades, is short of workers. Cities and factories swallow thousands of hectares of farmland every year. The writer asks who will grow the grain and what the educated young will do. Her answer is that both questions have one root: farming must become a technology-driven business, not a refuge of wage labour.

On divided and shrinking land, old methods will not yield more. Soil-moisture sensors, micro-irrigation, climate-ready seeds and AI are needed, and it is educated young people who can do this work. The difficulty is that farming is still seen as a job for the uneducated, and farmers do not want to send their children to the field.

The writer suggests universities become incubators for farm technology, where agriculture, computer science and business students work together. China consolidated small holdings into large farms, Australia adopted precision farming with GPS, drones and sensors, and the Netherlands dealt with a shortage of land through vertical farming and hydroponics.

If data sets the dose of fertiliser and irrigation, excess urea falls and groundwater is saved. Vertical farming near Dhaka and Chattogram can protect against floods and salt water. The writer says that when AI is changing jobs, food and land have become strategic assets. If educated young people come into farming, farmers can move from a subsistence trade to makers of new ideas.
nazar: This debate is a mirror for India too. Here as well the young are running from farming and graduate unemployment is rising in the cities.

Without changing the habit of treating farming as a subsistence trade, neither self-reliance nor rural jobs will come. The government's job is not only to distribute subsidies but to bring in the young who can put technology in the field.
sawal: Why do educated young people not turn to the field?
ref: Nabanna
The festival of the new harvest in Bangladesh, in the month of Agrahayan, which begins on 16 November.
Hydroponics
Growing plants in water with nutrients, without soil.

h: The Red Sea's safety runs through Yemen's state
dek: Yemeni researcher Nabeel Al-Bukairi argues that warships at Bab al-Mandeb will not bring shipping back to safety until Yemen's state is restored.
body: Yemeni researcher Nabeel Al-Bukairi writes that for ten years Yemen's civil war was treated as a merely local matter, but the attacks of 2024-2025 and this year have shown that the conflict now touches world trade and shipping. Houthi power has grown to the point of frightening ships passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and the writer says this is not merely a military event but the consequence of Yemen's state institutions collapsing.

He recalls that in September 2014 the Houthis took Sanaa and the remains of an army once reckoned the fifth largest in the Arab world fell into their hands. The world did almost nothing to stop Yemen from breaking apart. The 2018 Stockholm agreement deepened Houthi dominance over Hodeidah port, and the 2021 withdrawal of the joint forces on the west coast handed them a whole district.

According to the writer the biggest mistake was that the coalition backing Yemen's government built dozens of armed groups outside the state's command. The UAE backed the separatist Southern Transitional Council and Saudi priorities stayed different. The state that was supposed to be restored was itself weakened, and the Houthis grew stronger.

Today the Houthis have drones, ballistic and possibly hypersonic missiles, and more than 2,500 km of Yemen's coastline is under their control. The writer says warships and naval units can stop missiles but cannot change the condition in which an armed group strikes from Yemeni soil. Maritime security cannot be separated from the security of the state.

His solution is clear: put the state first, back legitimate institutions, bring the army and security forces under one command, end scattered power centres, and reach a political settlement only once armed groups like the Houthis have been broken. All Gulf states, including the UAE, must accept that their own security lies in restoring Yemen's state.
nazar: For India this is not a distant conflict. Our oil and goods for Europe pass through the Red Sea, and Houthi attacks have made shipping dearer. The writer argues for defeating the Houthis militarily, which is his own side of the argument; the lesson for us is that guarding ports must go with a political settlement in Yemen, or the guns will keep talking.
sawal: If Yemen's state is broken, whose hands guard the Red Sea?
ref: Bab al-Mandeb
The strait joining the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, through which a large part of Europe-Asia trade passes.
Stockholm agreement
The 2018 ceasefire on Hodeidah port between Yemen's government and the Houthis, which the writer sees as tilted towards the Houthis.

h: El Nino is forecast, the law is still silent
dek: Two South African legal experts write that despite warnings of a record-breaking El Nino, the protective clauses of the climate law lie switched off.
by: Ademola O Jegede and Patrick P Maweto
body: Two South African legal experts, Professor Ademola O Jegede and Dr Patrick P Maweto, say the weather service has done its job; the question is why the law is waiting. On 10 September 2026 the US oceans agency NOAA put a 75 per cent chance on this El Nino being the strongest since 1950 by December, and the ocean kept warming through October.

The South African Weather Service expects below-normal rain over most of the country this spring and record heat in 2027. Southern Africa is a climate hotspot, where El Nino brings drought, heatwaves, crop loss and a long fire season. The 2015/16 drought strained the preparedness of the Southern African Development Community, and in 2023/24 seven countries declared a national disaster.

According to the writers, South Africa's 2024 climate law was made for exactly this moment. Sections 17 to 22 require risk assessment, adaptation targets and provincial plans, but a 2025 notice has postponed them until the rules are framed. That means no municipality in Limpopo or KwaZulu-Natal has a legal duty to prepare for El Nino. The Western Cape is preparing out of choice, not obligation.

The second route is the 2002 disaster management law, which has so far been invoked only after damage. Cape Town's 2018 drought, the 2024 KwaZulu-Natal floods and the 2025/26 Limpopo floods were all declared disasters afterwards. Yet this same law lets the National Disaster Management Centre classify a hazard in advance, so that funds can open in time.

They have four demands: Parliament should notify sections 17 to 22, the Centre and the minister should treat a forecast as a hazard and declare a disaster early, the labour department should set a mandatory heat limit for outdoor workers, and every at-risk municipality should publish an El Nino emergency plan.
nazar: Several Indian states fight heat and drought every year, yet there is no mandatory heat limit for outdoor workers and no mandatory emergency plan for cities. South Africa's example shows that warnings arrive months ahead while the law moves at its own pace; paying compensation after the loss is not preparedness.
sawal: Everyone has the forecast, whose duty is the preparation?
ref: El Nino
A natural warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean that returns every two to seven years and reshapes rainfall across the world.
SADC
The Southern African Development Community, a 16-country regional bloc that coordinates members' drought and disaster planning.

h: A ceasefire declared, the war still standing
dek: Safia Southy, an expert in international law, writes that Gaza's ceasefire, by leaving return and governance to outside powers, can turn a temporary arrangement into a permanent one.
body: Safia Southy, a lawyer working on international law and war crimes, writes that the first anniversary of the Gaza ceasefire passed amid unfinished lives. Abdullah Abu Zubaida's family lives in shelter built from the rubble of its own house, and Ne'man Abu Jarad is still in a tent with five daughters, with no settled route home.

The writer calls it a zombie conflict: a ceasefire has been declared, yet Israeli military control and strikes continue. Her real argument is about the terms. Peace agreements do constitutional work, because they decide who governs, over which land and with whose consent. Handing the terms of return and Palestinian self-rule in Gaza to outside powers can make this arrangement a permanent external control with no fixed end.

This is not the first time. In the 1948 war some 750,000 Palestinians were displaced, 1967 brought occupation, and in 2005 the army pulled out while control of air and sea routes remained. In 2024 the International Court of Justice also said the duties of occupation had not fully ended. The Oslo interim arrangement was meant to last five years; thirty years on, the same framework is running.

The toll is staggering. According to Gaza's health ministry, 74,494 people had been killed and 175,604 wounded by 21 October. A United Nations commission said in October 2026 that genocidal acts continued even after the ceasefire. Israeli military control has grown from 53 to at least 60 per cent, and 217 camps face flood risk this winter.

Resolution 2803 of November 2025 put administration and reconstruction under outside supervision through a Board of Peace chaired by Trump. The arrangements hold until 31 December 2027, but there is no date for full return or the handover of power. In such a set-up whoever sets the standard stays the strongest, and even after weapons are laid down, return can be postponed.
nazar: Every postponed month in Gaza is another winter for a family, another lost year of school for a child, another delayed treatment for a patient. The lesson for the world is plain: declaring a ceasefire and making it real are two different things, and where there is no date, there is no accountability.
sawal: Who sets the standard for return, and will the ceasefire then hold?
ref: Resolution 2803
In November 2025 the UN Security Council endorsed Trump's plan for Gaza, including supervision by a Board of Peace and an international stabilisation force.
Board of Peace
A body chaired by Trump, given authority to oversee Gaza's administration and reconstruction.

h: Delhi's air improves, 39 stations still above 200
dek: Monday morning Delhi's average index came down to 216, but air at 39 stations is still above 200, and it is expected to worsen again from 17 November.
body: At seven on Monday morning Delhi's average air quality index was 216, in the poor category. A day earlier, on Sunday morning, it was 352, very poor. According to Central Pollution Control Board data, 39 of the city's 59 monitoring stations stayed above 200. Only two stations crossed 300 and no station recorded air in the severe category.

The worst air was at Sirifort, where the index was 346. Then NSIT Dwarka at 330, Pusa 282, Punjabi Bagh 276, Chandni Chowk 271 and ITO 267. The cleanest air was in the Cantonment, at 94. Delhi's air has been in this state since Diwali, when the capital stayed in the very poor category for several days.

This relief is not for long. Reports say pollution is expected to rise again from 17 November. That suggests the improvement on Monday morning was more a seasonal change brought by rain and wind direction. The daily grind over air quality in Delhi is not over.

The real warning for the city is those 39 stations still above 200. Among them are areas like NSIT Dwarka and Sirifort where the index crossed 300. Road dust, burning of waste and nearby units must be checked first in such places. Reading only the average and deciding the air is clearing would be unfair to the people in areas where breathing is still hard.
nazar: One day's improvement does not change the politics of air. When stations like Sirifort and Dwarka cross 300, an average of 216 is only good news, not a solution. The real question is when a station-by-station plan will be made, and who will answer for it.
sawal: Cantonment's air is 94 and Sirifort's 346. Why?
ref: Air quality index

0 to 50 is good, 51 to 100 satisfactory, 101 to 200 moderate, 201 to 300 poor and 301 to 400 very poor.
Above 400 is the severe category.
CPCB

The Central Pollution Control Board, which gathers air data from stations across the country.
The daily city reports are built on its figures.

h: Jharkhand: charges against an MLA, two commissions seek reports
dek: The women's commission has asked the DGP and the tribal commission the state government for a report, while the MLA calls the allegations false.
body: The National Commission for Women and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes have sought reports from the Jharkhand government on allegations that Bhushan Bara, a Congress MLA from Simdega, sexually assaulted a 14-year-old domestic help. The women's commission has asked Director General of Police Tadasha Mishra for a detailed report within seven days. The tribal commission has also asked for information on the case in the same period.

The girl is from Simdega district. She alleges that on 5 August the MLA raped her at his residence, after which she became pregnant. She also claims that a medical test later confirmed a miscarriage. On Friday an FIR was registered against the MLA at the Dhurwa police station in Ranchi under the POCSO Act and the Juvenile Justice Act. The police have had the girl medically examined.

Bhushan Bara, a two-time MLA, has rejected the allegations. He called them completely false and misleading. On Sunday evening the women's commission said on social media that it had taken suo motu note of media reports on 13 November. Commission chairperson Vijaya Rahatkar wrote to the DGP asking for an impartial, detailed and time-bound investigation.

The commission has also asked for an inquiry into the circumstances in which the minor girl was brought from Simdega to Ranchi on the pretext of getting her admitted to school. Directions have also been given to ensure the victim's privacy, safety and legal aid. The matter is in court and the charges are not proved, so the allegation must be called an allegation.
nazar: The commission's seven-day deadline is a good start, but if the report stays on paper no girl will get justice. The inquiry should also establish who took the child away from her home in the name of school, and why the victim's safety did not come before politics.
sawal: What evidence will the police show in the seven-day report?
ref: POCSO Act

The law protecting children from sexual offences, in force since 2012.
It makes concealing the victim's identity mandatory.
Suo motu

Taking up a case on one's own, without a written complaint, on the basis of reports or public information.
The women's commission often steps in this way.

h: Bilkis Bano case: two convicts' sentences suspended
dek: The bench released its 28 October order on 16 November, citing more than 17 years in jail and the serious disability of one convict.
body: The Supreme Court has suspended the life sentences of two men convicted in the Bilkis Bano gang rape and murder case and granted them bail. The order of the bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale was passed on 28 October and made public on 16 November. Both were also convicted of murder.

The court said both convicts have been in jail for more than 17 years and one of them is seriously disabled. The appeal involves questions of fact and law, so the sentence has been stayed. The trial court will set the bail conditions and the appeal will be heard in due course.

The case goes back to the 2002 Gujarat riots. The riots broke out after a train was burnt in Godhra. Bilkis Bano was then 21 years old and five months pregnant. On 3 March 2002 a mob attacked her family near Panivela, killing several members including her three-year-old daughter.

Both convicts had challenged the Bombay High Court's order of 4 May 2017. Their lawyer Siddharth Luthra argued that one convict was not named in the FIR and was made an accused about three years after the incident. The Gujarat government opposed bail. In August 2022 the state government had released all 11 convicts under its remission policy, but on 8 January 2024 the Supreme Court cancelled those orders and told all of them to surrender.
nazar: Bail for a convict who has served 17 years is part of the law, and the court has also recorded that the appeal is pending. But for Bilkis Bano it brings back the same old pain the whole country felt when 11 convicts were released in 2022. The speed of justice should be measured from the victim's side.
sawal: After 17 years, is age the only measure for bail?
ref: Remission

A reduction or waiver of sentence.
The Gujarat government used this policy in 2022 to release 11 convicts, which the court cancelled.
Suspension of sentence

A stay on the sentence while an appeal is heard. The conviction does not disappear, but the convict can come out on bail.
The trial court sets the conditions.

h: Wholesale inflation 12.29 per cent, fuel and power 32.84 per cent
dek: October's inflation figure stayed above nine per cent for the fourth month, while retail inflation reached a two-year high of 6.09 per cent.
body: In October India's wholesale inflation reached 12.29 per cent. This is the fourth month it has stayed above nine per cent. The wholesale price index for all commodities rose 0.70 per cent over September. The main reasons were fuel and primary article prices. The commerce and industry ministry released the figures.

The fastest inflation was in the fuel and power group. That rate, 25.85 per cent last month, rose to 32.84 per cent in October. The wholesale index for food articles fell slightly from 8.66 to 8.58 per cent. Inflation in manufactured products came down from 9.76 to 9.54 per cent, and core inflation stood at 9.6 per cent.

At the retail level inflation is sharper. Measured by the consumer price index it was 6.09 per cent in October, the highest in two years. That is above the Reserve Bank of India's tolerance band of six per cent. The food consumer price index was 8.94 per cent, up from 7.74 per cent in September.

According to Kanika Pasricha, chief economic adviser at Union Bank of India, the underlying pressure in wholesale inflation is stabilising, since the month-on-month rise was 1.2 per cent. She also said the pass-through of prices from wholesale to retail needs watching.
nazar: The 32.84 per cent inflation in fuel and power finally adds to transport and factory costs, so this figure is not far from the kitchen. Food inflation has come down a little, but retail crossing six per cent shows the relief has not yet reached the ordinary person.
sawal: Why is fuel inflation stuck at 32.84 per cent?
ref: Wholesale price index

An index measuring price change at the level of factories and wholesale traders.
The new series has 2022-23 as its base year.
Tolerance band

The RBI's target is to keep retail inflation at four per cent, with two per cent allowed either way.
Crossing six per cent counts as breaching the band.

h: Saharanpur: cane payments unpaid, farmers begin an indefinite sit-in
dek: Farmers of Ambehta Chand put up tents on the road against the Gangnauli mill, because the whole 2026 crop is still unpaid.
body: From Monday farmers of Ambehta Chand village in Saharanpur have set up tents on the Saharanpur-Badgaon road and begun an indefinite sit-in against the Gangnauli sugar mill. They are raising the issue of cane payments pending for two years. Angry farmers also did not allow the mill's cane purchase centre to open in the village.

Cane from about seven villages in the area is supplied to the Gangnauli mill. The farmers say the mill has only now begun paying for cane bought in December 2025, while the whole 2026 crop is unpaid. With no payment, children's schooling, the next sowing, and debts for fertiliser, seed and pesticide are all stuck.

Farmer Rajbir Singh Fauji said cane will not be allowed to be bought this time until the dues are paid. Rakesh Singh said the grievance was put to the district cane officer and every official, but nothing was done, so they had to take the path of agitation. He said cane is the main cash crop of this area and no one listens without payment.

The sit-in will continue indefinitely. Several farmers, including Shivkumar Singh, Mato and Sukhpal Singh, were present at the site. The farmers are angry with the mill and also with their elected representatives, because they say the dues issue has been raised for months with no firm answer.
nazar: Cane money is a farmer's income for the whole year. Holding back two years' dues may be the mill's compulsion, but the cost is being paid by the farmer's child. The administration should come forward not just to talk but to publish a date-wise account of the payments.
sawal: Two years of cane dues unpaid, who will act against the mill?
ref: Cane price

The state government decides how much the mill will pay the farmer for cane.
On delayed payment farmers sit in protest and agitate.
Purchase centre

The mill's centre where a farmer gets cane weighed and sent.
When it closes, the crop of several nearby villages gets stuck.

h: Winter session in the first week of December, delimitation bill up front
dek: Sources say the government wants to pass a constitutional amendment linking women's reservation to delimitation, for which it needs 361 votes.
body: Parliament's winter session may begin in the first week of December. According to sources, the government's biggest priority for the session may be the constitutional amendment bill linking women's reservation to delimitation. The proposal suggests delimitation could raise Lok Sabha seats from 543 to a maximum of 850.

That could open the way to implementing 33 per cent reservation for women in Parliament and state assemblies before the 2029 general election. Passing the bill needs a two-thirds majority, that is 361 votes. The House currently has 540 members, since three seats are vacant. The ruling NDA has 320 members, so it needs support from opposition parties.

The dates of the session are yet to be announced. The government has not formally ended the monsoon session. The session was adjourned sine die on 13 August and 94 days have passed since, but it has not been prorogued. That has also led to talk that a separate special session could be called before the winter session.

The government is also considering a formula under which the number of Lok Sabha seats could be raised by up to 50 per cent in all states. The final decision on both the dates and the agenda is still pending, so the opposition has little time to prepare.
nazar: The date not being fixed and the monsoon session not being prorogued both suggest the government is counting the votes it needs for a constitutional amendment. The figure of 361 is not easy, and the NDA will have to sit at the opposition's table. Making delimitation a condition for women's reservation will be the most contested part of the session.
sawal: Why is a delimitation condition being tied to women's reservation?
ref: Delimitation

The process of redrawing the boundaries and number of electoral constituencies.
The government says it is needed to implement women's reservation.
Two-thirds majority

A constitutional amendment needs two-thirds of the total membership of the House.
That is why opposition support becomes crucial.

h: Paramedics strike in Kathua, minister's convoy blocked
dek: Paramedical staff at five government medical colleges in Jammu and Kashmir are on a 72-hour strike, demanding that service rules be framed and applied.
ask: Frame and apply service and recruitment rules
body: Paramedical staff at five government medical colleges in Jammu and Kashmir began a 72-hour strike on Monday. There is one demand: that their service and recruitment rules be framed and applied. The employees say the demand has been pending for seven years.

Staff of the government medical college in Kathua took out a protest march to meet health minister Sakina Itoo. They stopped the minister's convoy for a while so that she would hear them. After police intervened the convoy moved past the protest site.

The minister told reporters there was no need for a protest and that work on the service rules was under way. One of the employees' representatives said they had expected a meeting with the minister but she did not listen. According to him, the minister stayed five to ten minutes but did not meet them.

The representative said staff of all five colleges are on strike because three or four years of repeated protests produced nothing. The employees say they were given a deadline of 30 September; 45 more days passed and no decision came. They warned that if the government does not act concretely, the strike will continue beyond 72 hours.
nazar: Seven years without rules, and 45 days past a 30 September deadline, suggests postponement has become the method. The minister's remark that no protest is needed sounds hollow to employees who had to sit on the road.
sawal: The minister stayed five minutes. Who heard the seven-year demand?
ref: Service rules

These rules decide recruitment, pay, promotion and regularisation of paramedical staff in government hospitals.
Employees say such rules have not been framed in Jammu and Kashmir for seven years.

h: Farmers sit in at Greater Noida, demand four per cent land
dek: Police stopped farmers marching to the authority office, so they began an indefinite sit-in at Happiness Park in front.
ask: Give farmers of 44 villages four per cent abadi plots
body: Farmers of 44 villages affected by the Greater Noida authority marched to its office on Monday demanding four per cent abadi plots. Police stopped them on the way.
The farmers then sat down in protest at Happiness Park in front of the office. A large number of women farmers joined. The farmers had already announced an indefinite sit-in at the authority.

Authority officials held talks with a delegation of farmers. The farmers said this time they would not go back with assurances alone. Their demand is that four per cent abadi plots be given to eligible farmers in exchange for land acquired, and that the matter be settled soon.

The farmers say the movement will continue until the demand is met, however long the sit-in lasts. According to them, talks and trust will not solve the problem. No fresh decision or official response from the authority had come out by the time this report was filed.
nazar: The land Greater Noida was built on has still not returned the farmers' four per cent share, and this has been the same for years. Every time talks and assurances, and every time the farmer on the road: that shows the matter is about intent, not rules.
sawal: Where did the 44 villages' share vanish after acquisition?
ref: Abadi plot

Uttar Pradesh provides that a fixed share of land acquired for development (four per cent in Greater Noida) be returned to farmers as residential plots.
Farmers of 44 villages are asking for that share.

h: Koch-Rajbongshi sit-in in Bongaigaon, demand for Kamatapur state
dek: A three-hour sit-in outside the deputy commissioner's office, with a parallel demand for Scheduled Tribe status for the community.
ask: Separate Kamatapur state and ST status for Koch-Rajbongshi
body: In Bongaigaon, Assam, Koch-Rajbongshi organisations held a three-hour sit-in outside the district commissioner's office on Monday. The sit-in began at eleven in the morning and the protesters raised slogans.
It was organised by the All Koch-Rajbongshi Students Union, the Koch-Rajbongshi Mahila Samiti and the Chilari Army. Students' and women's organisations of the district joined in.
Everyone's demand was the same: a separate Kamatapur state and Scheduled Tribe status for the Koch-Rajbongshi community. The organisations appealed to the government to meet these demands soon.

The Koch-Rajbongshi community has a large population outside Assam as well, in parts of West Bengal and in Bihar. Bongaigaon is in western Assam, where the Koch-Rajbongshi population is substantial. The demand for Kamatapur state is decades old, and ST status is seen as the route to reservation and a share in government schemes.
The organisations warned that if the government does not concede, they will intensify their democratic movement.
nazar: Statehood and status demands rising together in Assam show the community sees identity and rights as one fight. A three-hour sit-in and a warning over a decades-old demand is a signal to the government that the matter will not be postponed away.
sawal: Kamatapur is demanded again and again. Who will answer?
ref: Kamatapur
The old demand for a separate state for the Koch-Rajbongshi community, said to include some districts of Assam and parts of West Bengal.

h: Forest workers on hunger strike in Dhule over half pay cut
dek: Daily-wage workers of the Nandurbar forest department began a hunger strike outside the chief conservator's office in Dhule over eight to ten months of unpaid wages.
ask: Pay full dues without cuts, take back removed workers
body: In Dhule, Maharashtra, daily-wage forest workers of the Nandurbar forest department began an indefinite hunger strike outside the chief conservator of forests' office from nine on Monday morning. The movement is led by the State Forest and Social Forestry Workers Struggle Committee.

The workers allege that daily-wage workers in Nandurbar, Chinchpada and Navapur are owed eight to ten months' wages. They say 50 per cent of the dues is being cut by misreading a government decision of 13 August 2026. This, they say, is unfair to poor Adivasi workers.

The demands include full dues without cuts, immediate reinstatement of workers removed by oral orders, a record of a thousand days of work from 2004 to 2024 sent as a proposal for permanent service, and year-round work given the drought.

The committee says it gave prior notice of the movement to forest officials, the forest minister and the chief minister on 1 October, but there has been no hearing in a month and a half. Several workers, including Vijya Valvi and Muvasha Valvi, are on the hunger strike. District presidents of the Republican Party of India and the Vanchit Bahujan Aaghadi have extended support.
nazar: By holding back wages and cutting half of them, the department is only protecting its own accounts, at the cost of workers who planted its trees for years. A government that talks of saving forests should also look at how the family of the person who works in the forest is surviving.
sawal: By holding eight months' wages, what is the forest department saving?
ref: Daily-wage forest worker
Workers hired on daily wages for plantation and social forestry work of the forest department, paid by the day, with no secure service.

h: Port hospital to private hands, contract workers retrenched
dek: Taratala's centenary hospital has been handed to a private company, and CITU has opened a front over retrenchment and compensation.
ask: Take retrenched workers back, pay compensation
body: The centenary hospital of Kolkata port has now passed into the hands of a private hospital company. Retrenchment of workers on contract and agreement has begun since, alleges the Calcutta Port and Shore Union affiliated to CITU. The union protested on the hospital campus.

According to union leader Samarendranath Mandal, the hospital has more than three hundred staff, permanent and temporary, and their jobs are at risk. Built in 1969, the hospital with more than a hundred beds has been treating port employees, CISF personnel and their families.

The union says it complained to the state labour department, which said such retrenchment cannot happen, that those who lost work should be taken back and that compensation should be paid under labour law. The union is also preparing to go to court.

Port sources say the hospital has not been privatised. They say that to improve service only operations have been given to a private hospital on a PPP model, that beds will rise from 104 to 400 or 500 and that it will become a multi-speciality hospital. ETV Bharat called port public relations officer Sanjay Mukhopadhyay, who did not respond.
nazar: The administration says the PPP model will improve service, but the question is why improvement begins by cutting the jobs of people who have worked there for ten or fifteen years. Talk of compensation is hollow until it is on paper.
sawal: When three hundred jobs were decided, who was asked?
ref: PPP model
Public Private Partnership, handing operations of a public facility to a private company. The port administration says the hospital remains its property and this is not privatisation.

h: Tamil Nadu withdraws 600 cases against farmers and teachers
dek: Cases filed over peaceful protests between May 2021 and April 2026 are withdrawn, acting on the chief minister's assurance in the assembly.
ask: Withdraw all cases filed over peaceful protests
body: On Monday the Tamil Nadu government issued formal orders withdrawing 600 cases. These were filed against more than 90,000 farmers and teachers for protesting peacefully between May 2021 and April 2026.

According to a statement from the home, prohibition and excise department, the order follows chief minister C Joseph Vijay's announcement in the assembly on 2 September 2026 under rule 110. He had then assured that cases against farmers and teachers trapped in peaceful protests under previous governments would be withdrawn.
On the chief minister's directions the administration identified 600 cases filed between May 2021 and April 2026. Orders to withdraw them were issued after review under the laid-down legal process.

The order formally clears more than 90,000 farmers and teachers named in these cases. The decision comes at a time when, after a new government took office in the state, cases filed under previous governments are being reviewed.
nazar: The real question is that cases stayed registered for five years against 90,000 people who protested peacefully; withdrawal is relief that came late. Withdrawing a case is not the government's favour, it is the return of the constitutional right to protest.
sawal: 600 cases withdrawn, but why did they stay for five years?
ref: Article 19(1)(b)
This article of the Constitution gives citizens the right to assemble peacefully and protest. The cases against farmers and teachers were filed for using that right.

h: School hours changed, the bear's path was not
dek: Bear attacks have risen in Chamoli's forests, and the ones most in the line of attack are children who walk to school every day.
body: Rameshwari Devi of Pub Laga Vishal village in Chamoli's Pokhri tehsil went to the forest for grass and wood on 19 November last year and did not come back. The next day she was found clinging to a tree, unconscious, her face torn. She was flown to AIIMS Rishikesh, her face was put back together, but one eye could not be saved.

Bear attacks are not new here, but they have grown. According to Lahapath Negi, a pharmacist at the Pokhri health centre, five to seven cases had come by mid-2026, against only two in 2025. Forest department data show that in four years the number of people attacked rose from 57 to 71 and deaths from 1 to 7.

The biggest question is about children walking to school. Devesh Maletha (13) and Pankesh Agari (11) of Kailab village were on the path when a cub caught Devesh's leg. They got Rs 15,000 for treatment and he missed two months of school. On 22 December last year a cub attacked Aarav Pundir (11) while he was sweeping at school. Deepika held the door shut while the mother bear, searching for her cub, kept bumping into her. Two teachers found Aarav unconscious in the branches of a tree.

Amid official neglect the school management committee moved school hours to 7:45 to 10 in the morning. Teacher Upendra Sati says the forest department kept doubting their reports and hands cage-setting to fire volunteers. The department did not answer PARI's questions.

On 9 November 2026 the three children received Uttarakhand's first state-level child bravery award. Anthropologist Radhika Govindrajan says the conflict has grown in places because forests were cut for development projects, in others because abandoned farmland turned back into forest. The line between forest and field is shifting, but the village path is the same: a stick, a firecracker and trust.
nazar: More bears in the forest is counted as a conservation success, but somebody pays the bill, and it is the families living at the forest's edge. Changing the time children go to school was necessary, but it is not help, it is compulsion: without safety arrangements the whole burden falls on the elders and the children's courage.

In the hills the relationship between forest and people has been one of sharing for centuries, but development roads and abandoned farmland are spoiling it. The government must go beyond compensation and accept that the path children take to school is also infrastructure.
sawal: The school bell changed. Who will change the bear's path?
ref: State child bravery award

The first state-level bravery award for children given by the Uttarakhand government.
It was given for the first time in November 2026.
Himalayan black bear

The most common bear in Uttarakhand's forests.
A white crescent on the chest and long claws on the front paws are its marks.

h: Two in five children stunted, a kitchen only in 13,000 centres
dek: Madhya Pradesh's anganwadi data show that measuring children and reaching them are two different jobs.
body: Madhya Pradesh's children's health can be read plainly in the October 2026 nutrition tracker data. The state has 51,22,847 children under five registered, of whom about 99.62 per cent were measured for height and weight. Of those measured, 20,78,062 children are stunted, that is 40.72 per cent. Two in every five children are short for their age.

The number of underweight children is 11,88,901, or 23.30 per cent, and 3,55,419 children, or 6.96 per cent, are wasted. In October 2025 the stunting rate was 36.64 per cent and underweight 23.25. That is, stunting rose by 4.08 percentage points in a year.

This figure is not only about measurement, it is about the life ahead. According to the World Health Organization, stunting signals long-term undernutrition or repeated infection, and it also affects the ability to learn. Wasting often comes from illnesses like diarrhoea, which lower a child's power to fight disease.

The question is what happens after measuring. The state runs 97,882 anganwadi centres, but only 48,120 have their own government building. The worst state is the kitchen: a working kitchen is found in only 12,960 centres.

Of 65,90,347 people entitled to supplementary nutrition, 52,13,044 received food on at least 15 days in the month. That is, food is not reaching every entitled person on the register. In Khabar Lahariya's April 2026 report, children had almost stopped coming to an anganwadi in Kaidi village of Chhatarpur because there was no electricity. Schemes are running, but measuring and having a building do not fill a stomach; that needs a kitchen and regular food.
nazar: The data are clear and so is their meaning: the government is counting children, but the machinery to reach food to them is weak. When only 13,000 of 97,000 centres have a working kitchen, malnutrition will not be cured by filling in numbers.

The anganwadi is the last government link for village women and children. Its building, electricity, water and kitchen must be fixed first, only then will this stunting graph come down. This is not spending for later, it is the first spending to make.
sawal: 97,882 anganwadis, kitchens in only 12,960. Where are the rest?
ref: Stunting

Being short for one's age.
According to the World Health Organization it signals long-term undernutrition or repeated infection.
Nutrition tracker

The digital platform of the ministry of women and child development.
Anganwadi data record the nutrition status of children, pregnant women and mothers.

h: From a sinking home to Dhaka: Bangladesh's climate exodus
dek: DW's film uses one family to open up the picture that is becoming the biggest consequence of the climate crisis.
body: In southern Bangladesh, Lokkhi and her family are preparing to leave home for Dhaka before everything washes away. The compulsion is the climate: a rising sea, cyclones, storm surges and erosion. DW's film 'Black Water' uses this family to take the viewer to the Bangladesh the world still thinks of as a distant story, though there it is daily news.

Bangladesh's land lies very low above sea level and the delta of the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Meghna is the largest in the world. In such a place a small rise in the sea, a cyclone, a storm surge hits poor farmers, fishermen and daily wagers first. The government itself accepts that the monsoon, cyclones, heavy rain and floods will be more intense than before.

The film's question begins after the home is left. Every day thousands of people reach Dhaka, counted among the world's fastest-growing cities. How long can a city already packed with settlements, congested roads and long queues for work absorb so many people is a question no one can answer.

The projections are heavier still. It is estimated that by 2050 about 20 per cent of the southern coast will be uninhabitable and 30 million people will be displaced. The film's description also says Bangladesh's population will be about 220 million by 2050 and a large part of the country will be permanently under water. It is being called the largest forced migration yet.

This is not one country's compulsion alone. The countries least responsible for the climate crisis are paying the highest price, and that is why the demand for compensation and climate justice rises in Bangladesh. The film leaves one question behind: when the ground itself shifts beneath a home, who is to be held to account for the loss, and on which platform.

Nathso Leusa's film was made with the collaboration of Spain and Bangladesh and was chosen for the human rights category at Copenhagen's CPH:DOX festival. It came on DW in November 2026, and its centre is Lokkhi and her family.
nazar: For India this film is not another country's story. The Sundarbans, the Brahmaputra's erosion in Assam, the floods of Bihar and Bengal, the Odisha coast, all repeat the same arithmetic seen in Bangladesh. Those who leave home join the countless settlements of cities, and they are counted in no government figure.

The debates over climate funds and compensation have run for years, but the money must reach first those who have already lost their land, farming and home. Until then, climate justice will stay in speeches.
sawal: Who will pay for a sinking home, and in which court?
ref: Loss and Damage Fund

A fund created in 2022 to help countries devastated by climate disaster.
So far only small amounts have been deposited.
Ganga-Brahmaputra delta

The world's largest delta of three great rivers, which includes the Sundarbans.
Its land lies very low above sea level.

h: Everyone is angry with Gandhi. The question is why
dek: An American review of Ramachandra Guha's book shows that the way we remember Gandhi tells us what our politics is.
body: In South Africa a statue of Gandhi was attacked. In the United States, while statues of Confederate leaders were being pulled down, a university in Ghana removed its Gandhi statue too. These events are a decade old, but the question is the same: why so much anger against Gandhi?

Ramachandra Guha's book Arguments with Gandhi takes stock of that anger. In a review in the New York Times, Granta editor Thomas Meaney writes that the debate on Gandhi's legacy is no longer what it was. Some end it by calling him the father of the nation, others press him on caste and on non-violence.

What is interesting is that the reasons for the anger are opposite to each other. Some Hindutva voices see Gandhi as weak and as the man who divided the country. Dalit and Bahujan critics recall his politics of caste and his silence on it. Both sides build their own Gandhi and fight him.

Meaney suggests that keeping Gandhi in a museum like a saint is the biggest defeat we can hand him. Gandhi lived in argument, questioned his own decisions, and kept his colleagues with him even while fighting them. Making him an ideal is to abandon his method of reasoning.
Today every political camp borrows a Gandhi for itself. This book reminds us that Gandhi is not a legacy to be captured. He is a method, of asking questions and standing before power.
nazar: The debate about Gandhi is usually about his name, less about his method. The side that lifts him up as a saint is also the side that makes his questions harmless.
In Deshkaal's view, Gandhi's most necessary legacy is that he argued with power instead of asking for its consent. That argument is what we lack most today, and that is his real wealth.
sawal: Why do Gandhi's questions lose weight when he is made a saint?
ref: Arguments with Gandhi
Historian Ramachandra Guha's book, an argument over the disputed turns of Gandhi's life.
Granta
A British literary magazine, whose editor is Thomas Meaney.

h: Olinda: a city that grows inside itself
dek: In the eighteenth instalment of Calvino's Invisible Cities, the city does not spread outwards, it grows a new city inside itself.
body: Calvino's city of Olinda is found by walking with a magnifying glass. Look carefully and you may find a point no bigger than a needle's tip. Enlarge it a little and inside you begin to see rooftops, antennas, skylights, gardens, small ponds and flags strung across the roads.

That point does not stay as it is. A year later you will find it half a lemon in size, then mushroom-sized, then the size of a dining plate. And one day it becomes a whole city, one that had been living inside the city already there, and now begins to push it outwards.

Olinda is not the only such city. Like a tree trunk, many cities add a new ring around themselves every year. The difference is that in other cities the old centre stays where it was, with old walls and dry towers above it.

Calvino's Invisible Cities is a journey through more than fifty imagined cities, where each city stands for something else: memory, desire, a name, the sky. Olinda says that growing bigger is not only spreading outwards, it is also adding new parts inside.
Suman Shekhar's translation is appearing in instalments in Sammukh. Such serial translation of a whole book is rare in Hindi, and it gives the reader time to stop and enter each city.
nazar: We usually understand cities through maps and population. Calvino reads them as states of mind, and that is what keeps him necessary.
In Deshkaal's view, cities like Olinda exist here too: new settlements growing inside old ones, slowly pushing the whole city outwards.
sawal: Cities that grow from within, what do they look like from outside?
ref: Invisible Cities
Italo Calvino's book, in which Marco Polo describes imagined cities.
Olinda
A city in the book that grows new cities inside itself.

h: Jogen Chowdhury: an unbroken line in a broken world
dek: Remembering Jogen da, Garima Srivastava writes that the painter did not only make pictures; watering plants, he was looking and weighing all the same.
body: The lanes of Santiniketan, the house in Shyambati and the garden in front. Garima Srivastava remembers once seeing the great painter, white dhoti folded like a lungi, in a khadi fatua, watering plants from an aluminium bucket.

The man bent over the plants, absorbed, letting the water fall in a practised spray. From a few feet away it seemed he was taking news of every flower and leaf. Behind his spectacles his eyes held a tenderness for those plants.

Jogen Chowdhury was born in 1939 in Faridpur, now in Bangladesh. After Partition the family moved to Kolkata. After studying art he went to Paris, and then taught at Kala Bhavana in Santiniketan. The memory of Bengal's Partition returns again and again in his paintings.

He is called the master of the unbroken line, a line that draws a figure without breaking in the middle. His faces and bodies often look incomplete, frightened and restless, as if something inside were stuck and no way out were showing.
This piece is a remembrance after his passing. It holds not only the painter but the man: quiet, sunk in his work, and looking towards the people who often stay outside the light of the paintings.
nazar: This Bengali painter never saw the body as an ideal. His bodies are incomplete and restless, because the world he saw was itself incomplete and divided.

In Deshkaal's view, Jogen Chowdhury was the last of the great painters of a generation that watched the country being divided and then kept putting it back into pictures. His passing takes a part of that memory with it.
sawal: The line he would not let break, what did it say?
ref: Unbroken line
The mark of Jogen Chowdhury's art, a line that draws the figure without breaking.
Kala Bhavana
The art department of Santiniketan, where Jogen Chowdhury taught for years.

h: Belonging: the book that made noise before it was read
dek: Kunwar PrAnjal Singh writes that this book made so much noise before being read that every reader began to look for their own story in it.
body: The noise around a book before one reads it draws attention. Debate on social media, a crowd at Khan Market to buy it, and people of different ideologies lifting selected passages and interpreting them to fit their own understanding.

Kunwar PrAnjal Singh writes that such wide curiosity, interest and debate around a book is rarely seen. What is interesting is that everyone is looking for the story that suits them, and passages from the book have left its pages and reached social media arguments.

Read as the story of two lovers, a different world appears. How love for a boy slowly takes shape in a girl's mind, how attraction turns into intimacy and intimacy into love, is drawn here with great liveliness and humanity.

The reviewer recalls that very few memoirs open a different story from whichever angle you read them. This book is like that. As the pages turn, the story moves past its first meaning and turns towards questions of inheritance, memory and home.
The reviewer recalls a line of Arun Dev's, that this is not a book, it is a storm. That is why reading it as a mere biography would be unfair to it.
nazar: The debate began before the book was read, and that is the biggest truth of today's literary market: passages go viral, the book is read later.
In Deshkaal's view, this review is restrained because it looks at the book apart from the noise. The worth of a memoir should be decided by its language and honesty, not by its revelations.
sawal: Why is a verdict delivered before the book is read?
ref: Memoir
An account of one's own life, in which the writer sets down their experience and memories.
Khan Market
A Delhi neighbourhood with large bookshops.

h: Whose hands hold the measure of morality?
dek: Chetan Kashyap writes that in the literary field the measures of morality keep changing with opportunity, and the first to be questioned are those not close to power.
body: In the literary field it is not settled in advance on whom the measure of morality will fall. In this essay Chetan Kashyap sets out to test the very measures that are imposed on the literary world according to opportunity.

His example is the recent debate around the senior poet Alokdhanwa. One side says any discussion must keep his condition in mind, and many are busy declaring him ill. On the other side are those who invite him to their programmes and support his social participation.
Kashyap's question is who declares illness, and why. A writer who is to be removed from the stage is first declared ill. That is the language of convenience, not of morality.

The essay also holds some turns of his own life, which Kashyap does not hide. He accepts that several of his relationships did not last, and that a woman once told him he lacked social courage. He accepts that she was right.
Self-criticism and questions for others, both in one essay. That is the strength of this piece: it does not use morality as a weapon, it applies it to itself first.
nazar: In literary arguments morality is usually mentioned when someone is to be removed. For a writer who has power or a platform, the measures change.
In Deshkaal's view, Kashyap's essay matters because it applies the measure from inside, not from above. That is the right way with morality, otherwise it becomes only a sword.
sawal: Why is someone declared ill before being removed from the stage?
ref: Alokdhanwa
A major Hindi poet whose work carries the voice of the village, Dalit life and revolt.
Moral measure
The standard by which a writer's conduct is judged right or wrong, often a chosen one.

h: Chandrakanta's love letters: a big story of two small people
dek: In Neha Naruka's story Chandrakanta and Chandramohan are not big names, yet a whole village, a city and an era speak through their love and fear.
body: Chandrakanta was not worth lakhs and her man Chandramohan was not worth crores. Both were people of two cowries. That first sentence tells the whole temper of the story: no gods here, ordinary people, and the story rests on their love.

Chandrakanta kept getting threats of being married off to Jhiribhavanpura, Chandramohan warnings of scrubbing embroidery in some Bombay hotel. That is, before love stood not only the heart but home, village, earnings and compulsion.

The village in the story is a little metro kind of place: a paved road to the city, a high school, a few shops, fashionable girls, loafing boys and now and then a murder-mystery sort of incident. Jhiribhavanpura, on the other hand, is notorious for girls who marry into it craving greens.

The narrator opens these fears with a light hand. Her own relationship with greens is close, so she kept away from Jhiribhavanpura talk, but Chandrakanta was not like her. She leaned towards adornment and love.
Neha Naruka's language has the plainness of a village dialect, and also the sting that comes from the big city. The story is from her collection Mrityatmaon ka Desh (A Land of the Dead).
nazar: In small towns love becomes suspicion before it becomes big. This story is the script of that suspicion, where the honour of the house matters more than the girl's desire.
In Deshkaal's view, this story shows that sending a love letter is still a risk in villages. That voice is rarely heard in people's Hindi fiction, which is why it matters.
sawal: Where honour matters more than greens, how is love written?
ref: Mrityatmaon ka Desh
Neha Naruka's collection of stories, in which women of villages and small towns look for their place.
Shringar rasa
The rasa of love and beauty, in which secret lovers meet.
